Gale Brewer, Linda Lee and Members of the New York City Council Committee on Governmental Operations, State & Federal Legislation New York City Hall New York, New York Re: Hearing on the Non-Primary Residence Property Surcharge (“Pied-à-Terre Tax”) Dear Chair Brewer and Members of the Committee: My name is David E. Levy, and I am the President of 17-19 East 95th Street Tenants Corp, a 25-unit cooperative apartment corporation in Council District 8. I submit this testimony on behalf of our Board of Directors and shareholders. Our co-op supports the City’s goal of raising revenue from high-value apartments that are legitimately maintained as non-primary residences or investment vehicles. We recognize the need for a tax structure that asks owners of luxury, non-primary homes to contribute fairly to the City. However, we respectfully urge the Council to modify the implementation of the Non-Primary Residence Property Surcharge so that it does not impose disproportionate legal, administrative, and financial burdens on cooperative housing corporations and misplaced liability on their boards—particularly for small co-ops governed by volunteer boards. The problem is not the policy objective. The problem is the mechanism used to collect and enforce the surcharge against co-ops. Under the current framework, the City identifies the units deemed subject to the surcharge, but bills the cooperative corporation rather than the individual shareholder associated with the affected unit. The surcharge becomes a lien against the co-op property as a whole. In effect, a 25-unit cooperative and its other shareholders may be made responsible for a tax liability arising from the residency status of a single apartment. The City has effectively placed co-op boards in the position of tax collector, investigator, debt collector, and guarantor for individual shareholder. In addition, the current framework creates potential liability for co-op boards by imposing on them the obligation to forward surcharge notices to individual shareholders. For a small self-governed building, this is not a minor administrative task. Our Board members are volunteers. They do not have the staff, authority, expertise, or resources to conduct residency investigations, obtain and review sensitive personal tax and occupancy records, interpret trust and entity ownership arrangements, determine whether a lease qualifies for an exemption, administer appeals, or pursue collection from current or former shareholders. Yet the co-op faces direct financial exposure and potential legal liability if the surcharge is not paid. We respectfully request that the Council consider the following changes. Requested Changes 1. Bill and collect the surcharge directly from the affected owner or beneficial owner.

The City should issue the assessment and bill directly to the individual shareholder, beneficial owner, trustee, or entity owner associated with the identified apartment, rather than to the cooperative corporation. The City already makes a unit-level determination as to which co-op apartments are potentially subject to the surcharge. The collection process should follow that determination. If a co-op must remain part of the collection process for technical reasons, the co-op should be a notice recipient only—not the primary obligor, guarantor, or collection agent. A co-op should not be required to front a shareholder’s individual tax liability or expose all shareholders to a building-wide lien because one owner does not pay. 2. Provide an explicit statutory safe harbor for unit-specific pass-through and collection. The City and State should enact clear language authorizing co-ops to allocate any surcharge, interest, penalties, and reasonable collection or appeal costs exclusively to the shareholder associated with the subject apartment. This authorization should expressly supersede or clarify any concern that such a unitspecific charge conflicts with existing corporate, cooperative, proprietary-lease, or equal-per-share expense-allocation rules or NY State corporate laws. Without an explicit safe harbor, co-op boards are left to amend proprietary leases and create special assessments under uncertain legal authority. The City should not depend on thousands of individual coops to solve a structural statutory problem through private documents, particularly where lease amendments may require supermajority shareholder approval. 3. Protect uninvolved shareholders and the building from a building-wide lien. A non-primary-residence surcharge attributable to a particular apartment should not become a lien on the entire co-op building. At a minimum, the law should provide that the City’s collection remedies are limited to the shares, proprietary lease, distributions, and sale proceeds associated with the identified unit. It is inequitable to place every shareholder’s housing interest and the building’s financial stability at risk because of a tax dispute involving one apartment. This risk is especially acute in smaller buildings, where a single disputed assessment can materially affect cash flow, reserves, financing, insurance, and the ability to meet ordinary operating expenses. 4. Create a clear, independent, and practical appeal process. The City should provide a transparent process for challenging a DOF non-primary-residence determination, including: • Written notice identifying the factual and legal basis for the determination; • Meaningful time to respond and submit supporting documentation; • Access to the evidence relied upon by DOF; • Review by an independent tribunal or neutral hearing officer; • A clearly defined burden of proof and standard of review; and • A stay of collection and lien enforcement while a timely appeal is pending. Co-ops and shareholders need an appeal process that is understandable, timely, and independent. A process that relies principally on internal administrative review by the assessing agency is not sufficient where the consequences can include a significant building-level tax obligation and lien.

5. Limit retroactive assessments and protect subsequent purchasers. The City should adopt a firm and limited look-back period. More importantly, any retroactive liability should be collectible only from the person who owned or controlled the implicated unit during the tax year at issue. A co-op should not be liable for an earlier owner’s residency status after the apartment has changed hands. Nor should an innocent purchaser, current trust beneficiary, or remaining shareholders inherit an unanticipated tax obligation tied to a former owner’s use of the apartment. If DOF determines that a prior owner was subject to the surcharge, its remedy should be directed to that former owner or secured against the sale proceeds where feasible—not shifted to the corporation or a successor shareholder. 6. Provide standardized forms, guidance, and funding for compliance. If the City retains a role for co-ops in administering this surcharge, it should provide standardized owner certifications, trust and entity forms, notice templates, allocation rules, appeal procedures, and a dedicated DOF liaison for cooperative corporations. The City should also consider an administrative safe harbor for boards that act reasonably and in good faith based on shareholder certifications. Small co-ops should not have to hire counsel, tax advisers, and appraisers simply to determine how to administer a new unit-specific tax that the City itself has imposed. Conclusion Our co-op supports fair taxation of truly non-primary luxury residences. But the present implementation places a disproportionate burden on small cooperative corporations and their volunteer boards, while exposing uninvolved shareholders to liability for an individual owner’s tax obligation. The Council can preserve the revenue purpose of the surcharge while making it fairer and more workable by directing liability, billing, liens, appeals, and retroactive collection to the individual unit and the responsible owner—not to the co-op community as a whole. We respectfully ask the Council to adopt these protections and welcome the opportunity to provide further information based on the experience of a small, volunteer-governed cooperative in Council District 8. Respectfully submitted, David E Levy President, 17-19 East 95 th Street Tenants Corp New York, NY 10128 davidlevynyc@icloud.com Cc: Hon. Elsie Encarnacion

Linda Lee, Chair Committee on Finance New York City Council Re: Oversight Hearing on Implementation of the Pied-à-Terre Tax Dear Chairs Brewer and Lee and Members of the Committees: My name is Benjamin M. Williams. I am a Member and Head of the Property Tax Certiorari Department at Rosenberg & Estis, P.C. I represent numerous property owners affected by the new pied-à-terre surcharge. A pied-à-terre tax should tax pied-à-terres. This law can instead tax two things it was never supposed to reach: homes that are actual primary residences and homes worth less than $5 million. First, the law focuses too heavily on who owns the home and how title is structured, rather than on whether someone actually lives there. A New Yorker may live full-time in a home, pay City income taxes, vote in New York City, and list the property on an IT-201 tax return, yet still be denied primary-residence treatment because: • the property is owned by an LLC that is owned by a trust; • the property is jointly owned by two LLCs; • the property is rented to a corporation; • the occupant is a stepchild rather than one of the relatives specifically listed in the statute; • the owner is living elsewhere temporarily while a new primary home is renovated; or • a parent purchased an apartment for a daughter who is preparing to move in but had not done so by January 5. These are not pied-à-terres. They are not empty luxury apartments used only occasionally. They are homes occupied—or being prepared for occupancy—by New Yorkers. ROS EN BERG& ESTI S, P.C. The primary-residence test should be simple: Does a natural person actually use the property as a principal home? If the answer is yes, the ownership chain, entity structure, percentage interests, and precise family relationship should not control. An IT-201 listing the property as the occupant’s permanent home should ordinarily be sufficient. Alternatively, matching government records such as a driver’s license and voter registration should establish residency. The law should also provide a reasonable transition period for documented renovations and bona fide move-ins. Second, Phase One can tax co-ops and condos that are worth less than $5 million. The Legislature expressly stated that the surcharge was intended for second homes worth at least $5 million based on comparable sales. Yet during Phase One, co-ops and condos become subject to review at a $1 million DOF market value. That value is based on the City’s property-tax valuation system—not necessarily the apartment’s actual sale value. The $1 million threshold is only a proxy. Proxies produce mistakes. A co-op or condo owner should therefore be allowed to establish, through a recent sale, appraisal, or comparable-sales analysis, that the apartment is actually worth less than $5 million. If the owner proves that, the apartment should not be subject to the surcharge. The Council should press for two targeted State-law amendments: 1. Exclude any home actually used as a natural person’s primary residence, regardless of ownership structure or technical family status. 2. Create a Phase One safe harbor for any co-op or condo shown to have a sales-based market value below $5 million. The tax was promoted as a surcharge on extraordinarily valuable second homes whose owners do not contribute City income taxes. The current law is not narrowly written to reach that group. The rule should be straightforward: A primary home is not a pied-à-terre, and a home worth less than $5 million should not be taxed as one. Respectfully submitted, Benjamin M. Testimony from Ain Gordon re NYC Pied A Terre tax impact on Artist live/work space My name is Ain Gordon, I am a native New Yorker and a full-time non-profit theater artist living and working in NYC. My parents, David Gordon and Valda Setterfield were also full-time NYC non-profit dance and performance makers. Back in 1976 they used their modest savings (and borrowed money) to purchase a live-work JLWQA loft in Soho where I lived into my mid-20's and where they continued to lived till their deaths in 2022 and 2023 respectively. Throughout those years they performed, made and showed dozens of works in the studio portion of the loft. Throughout the past 40 years I have also created and showed all my work in that studio. Since their deaths I have rehearsed multiple projects there with public showings - as well as supported creation time (free of charge) for choreographer Emily Coates, theater maker Moe Angelos (with public showings) and choreographer Wally Cardona (including 5 weeks of public performances in 2025). I am also housing an 11-artist NYC LGBTQ+ Artist Archiving project there. In addition, Cardona regularly teaches technique class there, etc. However, because my primary residence is in Brooklyn (for over 20 years) where I live with my partner, near the kids we are raising together with their two mothers, I am now being charged more than 90K by the city's new Pied A Terre tax. I don't even make half that amount annually. I will be forced to sell as fast as possible - immediately depriving myself and roughly a dozen other artists of no-charge working space (I manage pay all the annual costs). I am asking that Live/Work artist lofts be considered as a different class – especially in a city where artist-friendly spaces are rapidly disappearing due to rising costs – causing many artists to leave - denuding a vital ingredient to our city’s cultural life. thank you so much, Ain Gordon

Thank you for considering this testimony. I recognize the desire to raise revenue for the City. However, I question the second home surcharge to the extent it may be applied to properties that are under renovation and genuinely cannot be inhabited due to unsafe conditions and lack of bath and/or kitchen facilities. I do not understand how City law can simultaneously prohibit people from living in places with no kitchen or bath (with good reason), but also tax them for failure to do so. Owners who are renovating appear uniquely negatively situated under the surcharge compared to others who can occupy the premises or rent, leading to a strange situation where a New York City taxpayer with a home whose value is just over the threshold may be exposed to the surcharge while someone with a far more expensive property who lives out of state is not. My understanding is that the tax is intended to penalize leaving second homes sitting empty, but this rationale does not apply to a property that cannot be occupied by anyone. The surcharge, if applied to renovating property owners, also produces irrational and arbitrary results based on accidents of timing that are not under taxpayer’s control – one family may be able to move in by January 5 because the Department of Buildings process goes quickly, while another cannot because the DOB takes longer. The City has permitting information on major renovations and could confirm whether a property has electricity, water, plumbing and otherwise can be inhabited during renovation for purposes of the second home surcharge. Discouraging renovation and purchase of properties in disrepair has detrimental consequences for the real estate and construction industries. I urge the City Council to act to protect constituents regarding this aspect of the law. Thank you.

To the Council:

I write in support of the pied a terre tax, despite glitches in its implementation. Many world cities like New York have had to create pied a terre and/or vacancy taxes or fees: Singapore, Paris, Vancouver, Melbourne, San Francisco, to name just a few. Empty high-end properties are a blight on the life of a city. They artificially drive up prices and rents, and leave us without actual full time residents whose activities could contribute to the economic and social life of our city. Whether the owners of these properties pay the tax or sell the property to someone who’ll actually live there, buying coffee on the corner and catching cabs, the city benefits. We’ve needed this since before the Bloomberg-based blight of empty superskinny towers began. Remember that you represent the city’s residents, please, and not its absent proprietors.

Alison Bardsley

Staten Island 10301

Dear NYC City Council,

My name is Amy Sophia Pinilla. I live at in Jackson Heights, Queens. I am a born & raised, lifelong New Yorker writing in strong support of the pied-a-terre tax and its full implementation. This tax is a critical step in the right direction to ensure that we fill our city’s budget shortfall, address the federal cuts enacted by HR-1, and ensure Mayor Mamdani has the money he needs to enact his wildly popular affordability agenda.

The federal government, through HR-1, slashed trillions of dollars from the social safety net in order to deliver the wealthiest Americans a massive tax break - and New York millionaires a $12 billion tax cut every single year. I’ve seen firsthand members of my family who relied on New York’s Essential Plan because of a lack of affordable options for healthcare lose their access to care within a matter of weeks. Now, I am supporting my family members in seeking alternative care but affordability is a constant debilitating factor. The pied a terre tax would raise $500 million in desperately needed funding, by taxing only the residences of millionaires who do not even reside there. This is the first step, and quite frankly the bare minimum our city can do to recoup that wealth and support New York’s most vulnerable community members. The City must implement the pied a terre tax to its fullest extent to stand with the working class residents of our state, and not the ultra-wealthy, and ensure our city is one where everyone can afford to live and thrive.

The pied-a-terre tax is only the first step. New York City is home to massive amounts of wealth being hoarded by very few, and we are the home of the highest income inequality in the entire country. It is long overdue to balance the scales of equity and tax New York’s ultra rich corporations and individuals and invest in what our communities truly need and deserve – accessible healthcare, universal childcare, free public education, beautiful and accessible parks and community spaces, affordable housing, and additional supportive services.

Thank you.

Dear Governor Hochul, Mayor Mamdani, and Members of the New York State Legislature: I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed pied-à-terre tax on New York City residences.

While the proposal may be presented as a tax aimed at wealthy owners of second homes, its real-world impact could be much broader and more damaging. It risks penalizing long-time New York property owners, depressing residential property values, discouraging investment in New York City, and placing yet another burden on a real estate market already carrying extraordinarily high taxes and costs.

Many owners who could be affected are not foreign investors holding empty luxury apartments. They may be long-time New Yorkers who own their homes through trusts, LLCs, family arrangements, or other ownership structures. Some have lived in their apartments for decades. Others may temporarily spend substantial time elsewhere because of family, health, work, or caregiving responsibilities. None of these circumstances should automatically transform a New York home into a taxable “pied-à-terre.”

New York City property owners already pay substantial real estate taxes, income taxes, transfer taxes, mansion taxes, maintenance charges, and other costs. Adding a recurring tax based simply on how a residence is

classified—or how much it is deemed to be worth— creates another reason for people to sell, buy elsewhere, or establish their primary residence outside New York.

There is also a serious fairness issue. A residence does not consume dramatically more city services merely because its owner spends fewer days in it. In fact, a lightly occupied residence may consume fewer municipal services than a full-time occupied home. Imposing an additional annual tax on that property therefore appears less like payment for services and more like a penalty for ownership.

The potential effect on cooperatives and condominiums is particularly concerning. New York’s co-op market is unique. Apartment values affect not only the individual owner but comparable values throughout an entire building. A tax that causes affected owners to sell, reduces the pool of potential purchasers, or makes New York ownership less attractive can negatively affect residents who would never personally owe the tax.

If the goal is to address housing affordability, lawmakers should pursue policies that actually increase the housing supply and encourage investment and development. Punishing existing homeowners does not create a single new apartment.

At a minimum, any legislation under consideration should contain strong protections for long-time owners, New

York residents, family and trust ownership, co-op shareholders, owners whose circumstances temporarily require them to live elsewhere, and properties that are not being held primarily as speculative investments.

New York should be encouraging people to maintain their homes, invest here, spend here, employ people here, and remain connected to the city—not creating another financial incentive for them to leave.

I respectfully urge you to reject the pied-à-terre tax and instead pursue housing policies that expand supply without unfairly penalizing existing property owners or damaging New York City’s residential real estate market.

Sincerely, Audrey Garr New York City

Testimony Before the New York City Council Oversight Hearing on Implementation of the Pied-à-Terre Tax August 18, 2026 Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony concerning implementation of New York City's new non-primary residence surcharge, commonly referred to as the pied-à-terre tax. I am the founder of Habitat Magazine, a special interest publication for co-op and condo board directors. Habitat has published information about board governance for co-op and condo boards and the professionals that serve them since 1982. I write specifically about a problem that has received less attention than the valuation and notification issues surrounding the tax, but which could have serious consequences for New York City's cooperative housing community. The new law makes cooperative corporations tax collectors for the City. That should be changed. I am not addressing here whether the pied-à-terre tax itself is good or bad policy. Nor am I suggesting that a shareholder who legally owes the tax should not be required to pay it. My concern is much narrower. If an individual cooperative shareholder owes a pied-à-terre surcharge, the taxing authority should bill that shareholder, collect the tax from that shareholder and pursue that shareholder if the tax is not paid. The cooperative corporation should not be placed in the middle. The Problem Under the legislation enacted by New York State, the surcharge attributable to taxable apartments in a cooperative is placed on the cooperative property's statement of account. The cooperative corporation is then required to collect the individual surcharge from the tenantstockholder. That means a private cooperative corporation — governed by a volunteer board of directors and owned collectively by all of its shareholders — has effectively been enlisted to collect a government tax owed because of the circumstances of an individual shareholder. This raises a basic question: Why should the neighbors of a taxpayer be responsible for collecting that taxpayer's tax?

The cooperative corporation must pursue that shareholder. There is a serious issue of whether the co-op’s budget must budget for it. It may incur management fees, legal fees and other collection costs. Questions can arise under proprietary leases and governing documents about how the charge should be treated, and whether a board is even allowed to collect this tax. There may be complications involving estates, trusts, lenders, transfers of apartments and shareholders disputing their tax status. More troubling still, an unpaid surcharge can implicate the tax account of the cooperative property itself. That potentially exposes an entire cooperative — including hundreds of shareholders who have nothing whatsoever to do with the delinquent taxpayer — to consequences arising from one individual's failure to pay a government-imposed surcharge. That is neither necessary nor equitable. Co-ops Are Not Taxing Authorities A cooperative corporation has legitimate responsibilities to its shareholders. It collects maintenance. It pays the building's real estate taxes. It services the building's mortgage. It maintains the property and complies with an extensive body of City and State law. But a cooperative corporation should not, and potentially can’t, be required to serve as the collection agent for a tax imposed on an individual shareholder because that shareholder maintains a non-primary residence. The distinction is important. The pied-à-terre surcharge is triggered by facts concerning the individual shareholder: how the apartment is used, where the shareholder primarily resides, whether an exemption applies, and the value attributed to that particular apartment. The cooperative board does not make those determinations, the Department of Finance does. Once the government determines that an individual owes the surcharge, the financial relationship should therefore remain between the government and that taxpayer. There Is a Straightforward Solution The underlying tax does not have to be changed to correct this problem. The State Legislature should make a narrow technical amendment providing that, for cooperative apartments:

The Department of Finance bills the tenant-stockholder directly. The tenant-stockholder pays the Department of Finance directly. If the shareholder fails to pay, the government pursues that shareholder — not the cooperative corporation or the cooperative p roperty as a whole. The cooperative could, where reasonably necessary, provide information enabling DOF to identify the shareholder and apartment. But it should not be required to collect, advance or guarantee the tax. An unpaid surcharge attributable to one shareholder should not become a liability or lien against the cooperative property as a whole. DOF Cannot Solve This Problem Alone This distinction is particularly important for today's hearing. The Department of Finance has already received comments raising concerns about the role imposed on cooperative corporations. DOF has indicated that the enforcement structure was established by State law and cannot simply be changed through City rulemaking. In other words, this is not merely an administrative problem that can be solved by asking DOF to write a better regulation. Albany needs to correct the statute. But the New York City Council has an important role to play in making that happen. What I Am Asking the Council to Do I respectfully ask the Council to formally urge the Governor and State Legislature to enact a narrow technical correction to the pied-à-terre legislation that: 1. Requires DOF to bill cooperative tenant-stockholders directly for their individual surcharge; 2. Requires DOF, rather than the cooperative corporation, to collect that surcharge; 3. Makes clear that a cooperative corporation is not responsible for advancing, guaranteeing or collecting an individual shareholder's surcharge; 4. Prevents an individual shareholder's unpaid surcharge, penalties or interest from becoming a lien or enforcement obligation against the cooperative property as a whole; and 5. Preserves reasonable requirements for cooperative corporations to provide DOF with information necessary to administer the tax. This change would not alter who owes the tax. It would not change the tax rates. It would not change the exemptions. It would not reduce the amount legally due to the City. It would simply establish an important and familiar principle: The government should collect a tax from the taxpayer who owes it.

A Problem We Can Fix Before It Becomes a Crisis The pied-à-terre surcharge is new. Its implementation is still underway. That gives the City and State an opportunity to correct this provision before cooperative boards, managing agents and shareholders find themselves embroiled in collection disputes and before an individual shareholder's delinquency creates consequences for an entire building. New York City's cooperative housing structure is unusual. A cooperative apartment is someone's individual home, but the underlying real estate is collectively owned by the cooperative corporation. That structure makes it especially important that government distinguish between an obligation belonging to the cooperative corporation and a tax liability belonging to an individual shareholder. The pied-à-terre surcharge belongs in the second category. Whatever one's view of the underlying tax, a shareholder's tax bill should be the shareholder's responsibility — not the responsibility of his or her neighbors. I urge the Council to make this correction a priority in its discussions with the Governor and State Legislature. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony. Carol J. My name is Beverly Solow. I live in Inwood, in northern Manhattan, and I’ve lived in NYC for 44 years. I’m a grandparent and a parent of 2 public school teachers. I’m also a lactation consultant and have worked to help countless new parents return to the workplace.

I want to see the revenue from the PAT tax go to schools and childcare. Properly funded, the school where my son teaches in Queens could: 1) have the resources to ensure students can read at grade level, 2) hire more teachers to lower class sizes, in accordance with the law, and 3) provide more tutoring hours for students. As it is, my son often tries to fill the gaps on his own time, with extra tutoring. Teaching teenagers isn't as stressful as the lack of resources! Some of his students are unhoused. The cost of childcare is one of the causes of homelessness. With free childcare, hopefully we will no longer have nearly 1 in 7 students living in homeless shelters.

On a personal level, I want my son to be able to continue to live in the city where he was born and raised. I want to be near my grandkids!

We, who live, work and pay taxes here, make this city a desirable place to have a second home. It seems reasonable and fair to ask those who don’t pay full-time income taxes here, but who have luxury homes here for pleasure, to contribute to the well-being of NYC, its families and students.

Dear New York City Council:

I am writing in support of the mayor’s proposed pied-a-terre tax. My name is Isabel Peñarand Currie. I am a PhD Candidate and researcher at the University of California, Berkeley, where my research focuses on public finance, land and property taxation, and city planning. I am also a New Yorker living on a very small graduate-student budget, where after paying rent and basic expenses there is not much disposable income left. I strongly support the pied-à-terre tax. My research has taught me that a city’s fiscal system is much more than an accounting mechanism. Budgets and tax systems are expressions of a social contract. They tell us who we believe should contribute to sustaining a city, who should benefit from its prosperity, and ultimately what kind of city we want to build. The extraordinary value of New York City real estate is not something individual property owners created by themselves. A $5 million apartment is worth $5 million in large part because it is in New York City: because of our subway system, parks, schools, cultural institutions, streets and public spaces; because millions of people work every day to make this city function; and because decades of public investment and planning decisions have made particular pieces of land extraordinarily valuable. In other words, urban property value is socially produced. It is entirely reasonable that some of that value should return to the public that helped create it. And that principle is especially compelling in the case of extremely valuable second homes. We are not talking about taxing someone struggling to hold onto their primary residence. We are talking about people with enough wealth to own a home worth at least $5 million in New York City in addition to wherever they primarily live. New York's existing property-tax system is not simply failing to tax wealth progressively—it frequently does the reverse. Recent research finds that apartment buildings are taxed at 5.67 times the effective rate of owner-occupied homes, the largest disparity among major American cities. The City's own reform commission found that a $500,000 to $750,000 home could face more than three times the effective tax rate of a $2.5 to $5 million home. Correcting some of that imbalance by asking owners of extraordinarily valuable second homes to contribute more is not radical economics. And it is not politically marginal: two recent polls found roughly two-thirds of New York City voters support higher taxes on millionaires. Those circumstances are not disconnected from fiscal policy. When we underfund childcare, transit, schools, housing, or other public services, the need does not disappear. The cost is simply transferred from the public budget onto individual households. Families pay more out of pocket, go without services, work additional hours, delay education, or give up opportunities altogether. That, too, is a choice about who bears the cost of maintaining this city. The pied-à-terre tax makes a different choice. It asks people who have benefited extraordinarily from New York City's tremendous property wealth—and who possess enough wealth to maintain

multimillion-dollar second homes here—to contribute somewhat more toward sustaining the city that makes those properties so valuable. If we want New York to remain a city for teachers, families, students, workers, and everyone else who makes it function—not simply a place to store wealth —we need a fiscal system that reflects that social contract. I urge the Council to support the pied-à-terre tax.

I have had the privilege of both working at the New York City Department of Finance, from 1990 to 1993, and later running it as Commissioner, from 2002 to 2009 — so I have seen how this department administers the property tax from the working level as well as from the commissioner's chair.

I should begin by confessing a nearly four -decade love affair with the property tax. It began in 1987, when I was a young associate at a Brooklyn law firm and was first introduced to this subject — and I have followed it, and very nearly every change to it, ever since. That is not a common affection, but it is a sincere one, and it is why I ask the Committees' patience for testimony that gets into the machinery of assessment. The details are where this surcharge will succeed or fail for ordinary New Yorkers, and I have spent a career caring about exactly these details.

I offer this testimony on the implementation of the non-primary residence surcharge — not on the wisdom of the underlying policy, which is a matter for others. The law is in effect; the first payment falls due with the January 2027 installment. The immediate question is whether the Department of Finance is administering the surcharge accurately, transparently, and fairly to the New Yorkers who are not its intended targets. In several respects it is not yet doing so — and, importantly, the tools to do better are already in the City's and the State's hands.

1. The City already holds most of the information needed to identify who does not owe. The surcharge applies only to properties that are not the owner's primary residence. The Department does not need to ask most owners to prove that; it can determine it from records it already holds or can obtain.

The Department itself administers several programs that require a home to be a primary residence — the senior, veteran, and STAR exemptions, and the cooperative/condominium tax abatement, the City's single largest property-tax break.

An owner who already carries one of these has already established primary residence through the very system the Department uses to grant the benefit. Those owners should be cleared first, not asked to prove again what the Department has already accepted.

Beyond its own records, the surcharge's own test rests on the New York State incometax return — the address a taxpayer reports as home. The Department does not hold that data, but the State does, and the statute expressly authorizes the two tax departments to share it. The State also administers STAR, which since 2015 has been delivered to new homeowners as a State-issued credit that the Department never sees on its own rolls — so even a home that receives STAR can appear, in the Department's records, to r eceive nothing. That is one more reason the State's records, not the homeowner's paperwork, are the right place to confirm residency. Between what the Department knows and what the State can confirm, the City could clear the large majority of these owners without asking them for anything.

I have described this approach in more detail in the writing referenced at the end of this testimony, and built a public tool that estimates how few properties are likely to owe once these screens are applied.

2. The published roll and the mailed letters were strikingly over-inclusive. When the surcharge was announced, the State estimated it would reach roughly 13,000 second homes valued at $5 million or more. Independent professional estimates at enactment clustered in the same range — on the order of 10,000 to 14,000 properties. Applying the statutory value thresholds to the Department's own data yields approximately 24,000 properties that even meet the value test — before the primaryresidence question is asked at all.

Against that backdrop, the Department published a roll of more than 900,000 properties — essentially every one-, two-, and three-family home and every co-op and condominium in the city — under a banner tying it to the surcharge, and mailed roughly 17,000 letters telling owners their property "may be subject." A list of more than 900,000, when the expected universe was on the order of 13,000, is not notice; it is the cause of the confusion this hearing is examining. The Department has since conceded that the vast majority of properties on the roll will not be subject to the surcharge. The roll should be limited to the properties that actually meet the threshold, with a plain statement that meeting the value threshold is not the same as owing the surcharge.

The over-inclusiveness is easy to underestimate until it is made concrete. These owners have never paid property tax and, understandably, do not expect a property surcharge to apply to them. Yet under the statute as enacted, a property-tax exemption does not carry over to the surcharge: each of these owners must affirmatively establish primary -residence use, or owe the surcharge, on the same deadlines as every other owner. When I have alerted institutions in this position, the reaction has uniformly been that the surcharge "cannot possibly" be meant for them — and that reaction is precisely the problem. If a foreign mission or a house of worship does not realize the surcharge reaches it, it will not respond by September 18, and will not appeal by March. I raise this not to argue the Legislature intended a different result — that is not before this hearing — but because the Council should understand that the surcharge, as administered, reaches a diplomatic missio n and a house of worship the same way it reaches a second home, and the notice and outreach have plainly not reached the owners least equipped to recognize that it applies to them.

4. The surcharge poses acute, unresolved problems for cooperative buildings. Cooperatives present the hardest administrative problems, and the rules do not yet resolve them.

Unlike a condominium, where the surcharge lands on the individual unit owner's bill, in a cooperative the surcharge is imposed on the cooperative corporation's consolidated tax bill and must then be allocated to, and collected from, the individual shareholders who owe it. If one shareholder does not pay, the board faces a bad choice: advance building reserve funds — asking every other shareholder to subsidize one owner's liability — or let interest and lien risk accrue against the entire building's tax account, because the surcharge attaches as a lien against the whole corporation. Many

Page 4 of 10

proprietary leases predate this surcharge and may not clearly authorize a board to bill it as additional rent, to impose late charges, or to treat non-payment as a default.

The timeline makes this worse, and the calendar is tighter than the December date suggests. The Department expects to issue corrected reports by December 31, 2026 — yet the January property-tax bills are mailed in mid-November, several weeks before those corrected figures are said to be final. So a cooperative either receives a bill before the corrected surcharge figures exist, or must reconcile a late-December correction against a January due date. Either way, it leaves cooperative corporations and their managing agents virtually no time to review the figures, determine unit-level obligations, notify shareholders, collect funds, resolve disputes, and remit payment. At a minimum, the Department should support an administrative extension of the cooperative payment deadline, and should provide managing agents who act in good faith on the Department's own data a safe harbor from personal liability. I respectfully urge the Council to press the Department on how a cooperative is expected to meet a January obligation on information not finalized until the last day of December.

5. Owners cannot verify the value being used against them — and the data should be public. Owners have received figures without the basis for them. The Department should publish, in downloadable form, the unit -level data needed to verify a surcharge determination, and should state plainly how it is calculating each cooperative's per-unit share — a calculation that is not transparent today and that managing agents report cannot be reconciled against their own records. A determination an owner cannot check is not one an owner can meaningfully challenge.

6. The avenue to contest the surcharge is untested, arrives too late to be a real remedy, and does not tell owners what to prove. The surcharge is imposed on market value, and the law does provide an avenue to contest that value: an owner may file an application with the New York City Tax Commission on Form TC107, on the ground that the market value is "excessive" — that it exceeds the property's full value — or "unlawful." I want to be fair to the agencies: this is a real avenue, and it is not gated by the effective-market- value limitation that applies to ordinary property-tax review. But as the surcharge is being administered in its first year, that avenue has three serious problems the Council should examine.

First, the Tax Commission is being asked to do something it has never done — review market value — for the first time, at scale, in its busiest season. In the ordinary property-tax system, the Tax Commission reviews *assessed* value; it does not review market value. The Department's own annual Notice of Property Value says so plainly: the Tax Commission cannot change an owner's market value. For the surcharge, the Commission is now being asked to review market value directly, for the first time, for potentially thousands of properties — and to do so in the very same filing season, and on the very same deadlines, as its regular assessment -challenge caseload. The Department and the Commission have added staff, but additional headcount does not by itself confer on an institution a competency in market -value adjudication it has

Page 5 of 10

never had. There is also no Department -level avenue to contest value, as there is for ordinary taxes; the only path is the Tax Commission. The Council should ask how the Commission will be equipped to perform this new function, at this volume, in its first year.

Second — and most important — the review comes too late to be a remedy at all. The filing window is open now, and an owner who received a notice may file today. But the surcharge is due with the January 2027 installment, and the deadline to file with the Tax Commission does not close until March 1, 2027 (Class Two) or March 15, 2027 (Class One) — *after* the payment is due. There is no indication that the Commission will rule on any application before the January payment date; indeed, because the filing period itself remains open until March, the universe of applications will not even be complete until after owners have already paid. The practical result is that an owner who believes the surcharge was wrongly imposed must pay it first, in January, and wait — likely until the following autumn or later — for a ruling, recovering the money afterward through a separate refund process only if the owner prevails. This asymmetry is compounded by a further one: the City charges interest on late payments, but does not, as a general matter, pay interest on refunds absent a court order. So even a fully successful challenge leaves the owner having financed the City's error, interest -free, for the better part of a year. A remedy that cannot operate until after the harm it is meant to address — that requires payment before any ruling, and returns the money without interest if the owner wins — is hardly a remedy at all. The Council should ask the Department and the Tax Commission to state plainly when surcharge applications will be reviewed, and whether any owner can obtain a ruling before being required to pay.

Third, the rules do not tell owners what they must prove — and this affects every property type. The law establishes that a value challenge succeeds if the owner shows the market value exceeds full value, but it does not say what documentation will establish that. A homeowner does not know whether recent comparable sales, a professional appraisal, or evidence of the property's condition will carry the day. A condominium owner does not know how to rebut a value the Department derived through its income -based methodology, which by design does not track sales prices. And a cooperative shareholder faces the hardest version of the problem: the value being challenged is a building -level figure imputed to the individual unit through a share allocation that the shareholder cannot independently verify, and that the Department has not published. The City should publish clear guidance — well before the March 2027 deadline — on what documentation will be accepted to establish full value for each property type, with specific direction for how a cooperative shareholder can meaningfully contest an allocated value.

I would add one point specific to cooperatives and condominiums, because it bears on whether the value avenue is a real one for them. In practice, an owner of a cooperative or condominium unit already valued above the threshold will find it very difficult to succeed in a value challenge — the room to argue that the Department's value is "excessive" is narrow, because that value is the Department's own long-standing figure,

Page 6 of 10

which the Department sets and defends. The result is that, for the property types on which the surcharge most often lands, the avenue the City points to as the remedy may be even less available than for homes. The Council should ask the Department and the Tax Commission to state plainly what an owner of a cooperative or condominium unit would actually have to show for a value challenge to succeed — and whether, realistically, that avenue is available to these owners at all.

I would add one point on the residency side of this, because it interacts with the timing. An owner who wishes to contest the Department's non-primary-residence determination has two routes: respond to the Department first and, if denied, appeal that final determination to the Tax Commission (which carries a modest 30 -day cushion beyond the March deadline); or go directly to the Tax Commission. But there is uncert ainty in the materials about whether an owner who does not respond to the Department at all forfeits the residency challenge for that year — with only the market -value challenge surviving. That ambiguity should be resolved and stated clearly in every notice, because an owner who guesses wrong may lose a right without realizing it. And whichever route an owner takes, if it runs to the Tax Commission, the owner will still have to pay the surcharge in January before being heard.

In short, the City has built the machinery of review — a form, a filing window, deadlines — without yet supplying the things that would make it a functioning remedy: a decision before payment is due, a defined standard of proof, and clarity about which doo r forecloses which right. I raise these as implementation problems the Council is well positioned to press the agencies to fix now, before the January payment and the March deadline arrive.

7. One procedural trap deserves its own emphasis: choosing the Tax Commission is a one-way door. Beyond the timing problems described above, there is a specific procedural trap every notice should disclose in plain language. The Department's portal appeal and a Tax Commission filing are not interchangeable, and once an owner files with the Tax Commission, the Department's portal appeal closes and cannot be reopened. An owner who files with the Tax Commission believing it preserves every option may find they have foreclosed the Department-level path. Few owners will understand this from the current materials. Every notice, form, and guidance document should state it clearly, and the appeal window — currently very short given the confusion the notices themselves created — should be long enough for an owner to receive notice, gather documents, and seek advice before choosing a forum they cannot later change.

8. The City should confirm — and where necessary provide — payment plans for the surcharge, with favorable terms for those who will feel it most. A distinct problem follows directly from the timing described above: the surcharge is due all at once, with the January 2027 installment, and for many owners it arrives as a payment shock. This is most severe in two situations, and the City should address both.

Page 7 of 10

Capped properties where the surcharge exceeds the regular tax. The payment shock tracks one feature above all: whether a property is *capped*. For one-, two-, and threefamily homes and for the small cooperatives and condominiums in buildings of fewer than eleven units, assessment caps mean the owner has, for years, paid tax on a compressed value well below full market value — while the surcharge is imposed on full market value. Using the Department's own values, and before accounting for exemptions or abatements, the surcharge would exceed the property's *entire* regular property-tax bill for roughly 84 percent of over-threshold one-to-three-family homes (5,690 of about 6,800) and roughly 92 percent of over -threshold small (Class 2C) condominium units (2,234 of about 2,400), and roughly 96 percent of over-threshold small (Class 2C) cooperative units (834 of 866) . By contrast, among condominiums and cooperatives that are *not* capped — whose tax already reflects near-full value — the surcharge rarely exceeds the tax. Exemptions will, properly, remove many of these properties from the surcharge altogether; this is not a prediction that thousands of owners will be billed. But for the capped owners who do remain subject, it shows the magnitude of what arrives in a single January installment: not an increment on the tax, but a charge larger than the tax itself. That this same pattern appears across all three capped property types — homes, small condominiums, and small cooperatives, at 84, 92, and 96 percent — and in two independent measures, the share whose surcharge exceeds their tax and the share whose effective market value falls below the surcharge threshold, underscores that it is a structural feature of layering a full- value surcharge on a capped tax base, not an artifact of one calculation or one property type.

Cooperatives. As described above, in a cooperative the surcharge is imposed on the corporation's bill, must be collected from individual shareholders, and attaches as a lien against the entire building. A payment plan for the surcharge portion would let a cooperative spread the obligation and manage a shareholder who cannot immediately pay, rather than advancing building reserves or letting lien risk accrue against every shareholder.

I recommend the Council press the Department to (1) confirm plainly that an owner may enter a payment plan for the surcharge portion of the bill while remaining current on regular property taxes — which is not clear on the face of the rules, given that the surcharge is structured as separate from the property tax; (2) provide favorable terms where the burden is most acute, recognizing that a plan carrying the highest interest rate the Department charges, which reaches sixteen percent for higher -value properties, is not meaningful relief; and (3) make clear how a payment plan interacts with a pending challenge and a possible refund, so that an owner need not choose between paying and preserving a challenge. These measures do not change who owes the surcharge; they ensure that the New Yorkers who do owe it, and the cooperatives that must collect it, are not pushed into avoidable distress by the timing of a single January bill.

9. Phase 2 deserves its own dedicated hearing — but not at the expense of getting Phase 1 right now.

Page 8 of 10

Phase 2, beginning July 1, 2028, moves all covered property types to a single $5 million threshold based on a comparable- sales methodology. How the Department will derive comparable-sales values for cooperative units — which are not separately assessed and do not convey as real property — is genuinely unresolved and deserves close, dedicated attention with stakeholders before that methodology takes effect. I would respectfully suggest the Council hold a separate, future hearing focused on Phase 2 valuation, so that the urgent work of administering Phase 1 correctly for the January 2027 payment receives the full attention it needs right now.

Recommendations: what the City can do now The Committees asked, in effect, whether the surcharge is being administered well, and where it can be improved before the January 2027 payment and the March 2027 deadlines arrive. The problems I have described are administrable — none requires amending the statute. I respectfully offer the following action steps the Council can press the Department of Finance and the Tax Commission to take:

1. Clear owners the City can already identify. Use the Department's own records — the senior, veteran, and STAR exemptions and the cooperative/condominium abatement — and the State income-tax and STAR data the statute authorizes, to clear known primary residents first, rather than asking them to prove what the City has already accepted.

2. Correct the roll. Limit the published roll to properties that actually meet the value threshold, and state plainly that meeting the threshold is not the same as owing the surcharge.

3. Reach the owners who don't know it applies. Direct notice and outreach specifically to fully tax-exempt owners — religious, charitable, educational, and diplomatic — who do not expect a property surcharge to reach them and will otherwise miss the deadlines.

4. Fix the cooperative timeline and exposure. Support an administrative extension of the cooperative payment deadline, given that corrected figures are not final until December 31 while payment is due in January, and provide managing agents who act in good faith on the Department's own data a safe harbor from personal liability.

5. Publish the data owners need to verify their determinations. Release the unit level data in downloadable form, and state how each cooperative's per -unit share is calculated, so that a determination can actually be checked.

6. Make the review a real remedy. State plainly when the Tax Commission will review surcharge applications and whether any owner can obtain a ruling before being required to pay; and address the pay-first asymmetry — whether by accelerating determinations, allowing deferral pending a challenge, or paying interest on surcharge refunds as the City charges interest on late payments.

Page 9 of 10

7. Define the standard of proof. Publish clear guidance, well before the March deadline, on what documentation will establish full value for each property type — homes, condominiums, and cooperatives — with specific direction for how a cooperative shareholder can contest an allocated value.

8. Disclose the procedural traps. State clearly, in every notice and guidance document, that filing with the Tax Commission permanently closes the Department's portal appeal, and resolve and disclose whether not responding to the Department forfeits the residency challenge; and lengthen the appeal window so owners can act before choosing a forum they cannot change.

9. Provide payment relief for capped owners. Confirm that owners may enter a payment plan for the surcharge portion of the bill, on reasonable terms, with particular attention to capped properties — for which the surcharge exceeds the entire regular tax for the great majority of owners — and to cooperatives.

10. Give Phase 2 its own hearing. Commit to a separate, future hearing on the Phase 2 comparable-sales methodology, and to publishing that methodology — particularly for cooperative and condominium units — before it takes effect, so that getting Phase 1 right receives full attention now.

To support this work, I have made two tools publicly available that the Committees and their staff may find useful. The first lets the user estimate the surcharge's revenue under their own assumptions about how many properties are genuinely subject — a way for the Committees to test the City's revenue projections against their own judgment rather than taking them as given. The second helps an individual owner, or a constituent-services office assisting one, work through whether the surcharge applies and what would need to be submitted. Both are linked at the close of this testimony, and I offer them, and myself, as a resource.

Closing I offer this testimony because I care deeply about how this City administers its taxes, and because I believe the Department can do this well with the information it and the State already hold.

Rather than starting with readily available information that would easily demonstrate that we are full-time New York City residents, including our voting and tax records, the Department of Finance has eVectively presumed the opposite and placed the burden on us to “prove” that we actually live in our own home.

We understand and, in principle, support the policy goal of ensuring that tax benefits intended for primary residences go to actual New York City residents. But there is something deeply wrong with an implementation process that makes those very residents, New Yorkers who truly care about their city and neighbors, feel as though they are under suspicion. New Yorkers, like us, who regularly vote, pay their taxes, participate in their communities, and make this city their home should not receive letters from our city government that begins with the presumption that they may not actually live here.

We are particularly concerned because we cannot possibly be the only homeowners in the neighborhood to have received such a letter. If the Department of Finance is broadly sending these notices to legitimate primary residents without first making reasonable use of information and data already available to the City, then this is more than an individual inconvenience. It is a flawed process and issue that deserves your immediate attention and leadership.

We respectfully ask that your oVice look into how these notices are being generated, raise concerns directly with the Department of Finance and its Commissioner, and press them to establish a process that is more accurate, reasonable, and respectful of longtime New York City residents. At a minimum, the Department of Finance must make appropriate use of information already in its possession before requiring longtime residents, like us, to prove that our homes are, in fact, our homes. They need to do the work.

We care deeply about New York City and about our neighborhood. We love our open streets; we love the community we've built here in Brooklyn. We take seriously the responsibilities that come with being members of this community. In return, we expect our City government to treat us, and our neighbors, with the same basic measure of respect.

We would greatly appreciate hearing from your oVice about what steps you can take to address both our individual situation and the broader process that led to this notice.

Thank you in advance for your time and attention to this very serious issue.

Sincerely, Virginia and Marc Abrams

Good afternoon, Majority Leader Abreu, members of the Finance Committee, and members of the City Council. My name is Richard Lee, and I am the commissioner of the New York City Department of Finance. I am joined today by Annette Hill, Deputy Commissioner of Customer Operations. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the proposed ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program authorizing legislation. The goal of the ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program is to encourage the resolution ofECB violations to increase compliance and collect fines in an area that is difficult for the City to enforce. As a reminder, Environmental Control Board, or ECB, violations are issued by more than a dozen city agencies and cover a wide range of offenses, including dirty sidewalks, littering, failure to remove ice or snow, working without a permit from the Department of Buildings, and many other quality-of-life and environmental ISsues. Agencies that issue violations include DOB, DSNY, FDNY, DEP, DOT, NYPD, HPD, DOHMH, DCWP, and Parks. Violation recipients are typically businesses and property owners, but other individuals may be issued violations if they have committed an offense. ECB debt is referred to the Department of Finance upon OATH's docketing of unresolved violations that have been adjudicated by OATH's ECB sub-division. The proposed amnesty program would incentivize resolution and payment by reducing fines for people who have violations in judgment. Violations go into judgment when recipients do not pay or dispute them within 100 days, generally. Amnesty program participants would receive a 25% reduction in the violation amount and will have their interest waived. The program would require the resolution of any outstanding violations which require correction. The ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program was included in the Adopted Budget for $25 million and is modeled after previous programs administered by the Department of Finance over the past ten years. Such programs are particularly useful when the city does not have a strong mechanism for enforcement-unlike, Page 2 of3

for example, our boot and tow program for parking tickets, where customers must resolve their debt in order to recover a vehicle. The amnesty program would be open for 90 days, with an option to extend to 180 days. Please note that idling violations will not be eligible for amnesty, to ensure that we continue to hold bad actors accountable when they pollute our streets. Additionally, the main recipients of idling violations are logistics companies, who are less in need of amnesty. Developing a broad and simple program is the best way to achieve significant participation, and, ultimately, resolve more violations throughout the city. Thank you for your partnership, and I look forward to taking your questions. Page 3 of3

To Whom It May Concern,

I am writing on behalf of the ownership of the properties located at 53-20 46th Street and 23-54 Avenue in Queens.

I would like to clarify for the record that these properties are not vacant or underutilized. They have been used by our family and our business since at least the 1960s and continue to serve active industrial purposes today.

Because these properties operate in conjunction with one another, the loss of either site would create significant operational challenges. Relocating this type of industrial use would be difficult, as suitable outdoor storage locations that meet zoning and safety requirements are limited.

We understand the City’s goals in expanding public open space. However, we respectfully request that these properties be removed from consideration for future acquisition, given their long-standing, continuous use and their role in supporting local employment and business operations.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely, John Zak (on behalf of ownership)
